study.title: Esther 5 savour before the king and the fury of Haman
study.overview: Esther 5 shows a decisive turn in the narrative. After the fast, Esther presents himself to the king with courage, finds favor and postpones his request for a moment prepared by her. At the same time, Haman comes out of the presence of the queen exalted by her position, but her joy is poisoned by Mordecai's refusal to honor him. The chapter contrasts the serenity of Esther, who acts with prudence and respect, with the uncontrolled pride of Haman, who transforms a real honor into an occasion for more violence.

outline.title: Esther enters the presence of the king and receives favor
outline.explanation: On the third day, Esther dresses in the royal robes and puts himself in the inner courtyard, risking his life by appearing before the king without being called. The king receives it with favor and offers him the golden scepter, a sign of welcome. When he promises to respond to his request, Esther does not reveal everything immediately; she preserves the moment and shows discernment by not rushing his petition.

outline.title: The first banquet and postponement of the request
outline.explanation: Esther invites the king and Haman to a banquet, demonstrating care and strategy. Even with the king's new offer for her to ask her what she desires, she asks for another occasion and promises to speak the next day. The text highlights his reverent posture and his prudence, without revealing the real cause of his supplication.

outline.title: Haman's vanity and the plan against Mordecai
outline.explanation: Haman leaves the proud banquet, but Mardecai's mere lack of reverence destroys his satisfaction. When gathering family and friends, he displays his riches, his children and his promotion, but everything seems insufficient to him while Mordecai remained alive and free. The advice of Zeres and friends is to build a very high stake to expose and kill Mordecai, and Haman accepts the proposal promptly.

study.context: The chapter is set at the Persian court around the king, Esther, Haman, and Mordecai. The text shows palatial customs such as restricted access to the king, the use of the scepter as a sign of acceptance and the realization of banquets with wine as a formal environment of negotiation. It is not necessary to state more than the chapter itself provides: Esther approaches the king at real risk, and Haman occupies a position of honor at the court.
study.theology: The chapter highlights God's providence indirectly, through favor, timing and reversal of expectations. Esther does not act with precipitation; his courage is accompanied by discernment and respect. The king appears as an authority that can grant favor, but his disposition does not explain everything that happens. In contrast, Haman embodies the pride that is never satisfied: honor, wealth and promotion do not heal a heart dominated by wrath and self-exalting. The text also suggests that Mardoqueu's silent fidelity has spiritual and moral weight, even though he does not speak in this chapter. For an evangelical reading, the passage reminds us that God acts by ordinary and extraordinary means to preserve his people, even when their action is not explicitly mentioned.

scholarViews.insight: The observation that the king extended the golden scepter shows that Esther was not punished for entering without being called; the king's favor preserves his life.
The chapter contrasts Esther's joy and the irritation of Haman, teaching that those who sow in tears reap in joy, while the triumph of the ungodly is brief.
The description of the "winner" shows that Esther does not yet reveal his petition; she chooses the appropriate time to speak.

questions: What does Esther's courage teaches about obeying God with reverence and prudence at the same time?
Why can't the honor received by Haman fail to satisfy him when he finds opposition from Mordecai?
How does this chapter help us to perceive the difference between godly trust and a proud self-reliance?
study.practice: This chapter calls the reader to unite courage and wisdom. In difficult situations, it is not enough to act with impulse; one must seek the right time, speak with respect and trust that God can open improbable doors. At the same time, he warns us against resentful pride: we can accumulate achievements and still live dissatisfied, if a single injury to the ego dominates the heart. In practice, it is worth examining where we have postponed a necessary conversation for fear, and also where our joy depends more on human approval than on fidelity to God.
study.uncertainty: The text does not explicitly mention God, prayer or direct supernatural intervention in this chapter, although the whole of the book allows a providential reading. It is also not possible to affirm with certainty, only from these notes, the exact form of the "forca" or stake described, nor to detail Persian customs beyond what the text itself and the comments summarize. The king's language over half of the kingdom is recognized in the notes as a conventional expression of generosity, not as a literal promise of division of the kingdom.
